To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the AMI Large Array images of L675 show the presence of a deeply embedded protostar and the AMI Small and Large Array images of the Lynds Dark Nebulas L675, L1103 and L1111 show that spinning dust emission is correlated with 8 µm Spitzer emission.

(a) we find that the 8 μ m and 850 μ m emission in the dark cloud L675 are associated with a deeply embedded source and (b) we show that the 8 μm and 16 GHz emission in the dark nebula L1246 are spatially correlated, which is evidence that the spinning dust emission is associated with the 8 μ m emission.

(1) we have identified a deeply embedded protostar in L675, (2) we have found that the 8 μM emission in L1246 is spatially correlated to cm-wave spinning dust emission and (3) we have found evidence that the 8 μM emission in L1111 is due to a stellar wind.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the nature of the emission mechanism responsible for the excess of emission seen in the AMI Small Arrays maps of the five Lynds Dark nebulae.
the nature and origin of the anomalous microwave emission (AME) seen in the diffuse interstellar medium.
the nature of the emission mechanisms responsible for the excess of emission seen at microwave frequencies relative with respect to lower frequency radio observations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the spinning dust emission is not a universal phenomenon in molecular clouds, but is a localized effect.
we see the first clear detection of a stellar wind from a deeply embedded young star.
we have detected the cm-wave emission from L675 to be a young stellar object, L1246 to be a star forming region and the other three sources (L944, L1101 and L1111) to be star forming regions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cm-wave emission arises from a combination of free–free emission and spinning dust emission.
spinning dust emission can be spatially correlated with mid-infrared emission and can also be associated with stellar outflows.
the AMI images show that the spinning dust emission is spatially coincident with 850 μmsubmillimetre emission, 8 μmmid-infrared emission and 1.4 GHz radio emission.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cm-wave emission from spinning dust is likely to arise in a small number of dense regions within the molecular cloud.

the spinning dust emission seen in these objects is spatially correlated to 8 μmspitzerband 4 emission, which is a good tracer of polycyclic hydrocarbons, and is also spatially correlated to the 850 μm emission seen with SCUBA.
the cm-wave excess in L675 and L1246 is likely to be associated with the star-forming regions and not with the diffuse interstellar medium.
